lib.t: Note any vaccines that are due, using your health record, app or vaccination card. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure which vaccines are recommended for your age.
lib.why: Knowing which vaccines are due for you is a simple first step to staying protected.

lib.w: Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) to your face, neck and hands
lib.t: Keep sunscreen next to your toothbrush or moisturiser so it becomes part of your morning routine.
lib.why: Daily sunscreen on your face, neck and hands helps keep your skin looking younger for longer.
lib.ref: Hughes, M. C., Williams, G. M., Baker, P., & Green, A. C. (2013). Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine, 158(11), 781–790. https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-158-11-201306040-00002

lib.w: Apply sunscreen to skin that will be in the sun
lib.t: Use about a teaspoon for your face and neck and apply it before going out. Reapply every couple of hours outdoors and after swimming or sweating.
lib.why: Daily sunscreen on sun-exposed skin may lower your melanoma risk and slow skin ageing.
lib.ref: Green, A. C., Williams, G. M., Logan, V., & Strutton, G. M. (2011). Reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use: randomized trial follow-up. lib.w: Avoid sunbeds and protect your skin with shade, clothing and sunscreen
lib.d: every day the sun is strong
lib.t: Skip sunbeds and tanning beds altogether. On sunny days, seek shade in the middle of the day and wear a hat, sunglasses and covering clothing as well as sunscreen.
lib.why: Skipping sunbeds and protecting your skin outdoors work together to lower melanoma risk.
lib.ref: Boniol, M., Autier, P., Boyle, P., & Gandini, S. (2012). Cutaneous melanoma attributable to sunbed use: systematic review and meta-analysis. lib.w: Check the UV index before spending time outdoors
lib.t: Most weather apps show it. When it's 3 or higher, plan shade, a hat and sunscreen.
lib.why: Knowing the UV index tells you when your skin needs extra protection.
lib.ref: Dennis, L. K., Vanbeek, M. J., Beane Freeman, L. E., Smith, B. J., Dawson, D. V., & Coughlin, J. A. (2008). Sunburns and risk of cutaneous melanoma: does age matter? A comprehensive meta-analysis. Annals of Epidemiology, 18(8), 614–627. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2008.04.006

lib.w: Avoid sunburn by using shade, a hat and clothing as well as sunscreen
lib.d: every day the sun is strong
lib.t: Take a hat and a light layer when you go out, and look for shade, especially in the middle of the day.
lib.why: Avoiding sunburn, at any age, is one of the most direct ways to protect your skin.
lib.ref: Dennis, L. K., Vanbeek, M. J., Beane Freeman, L. E., Smith, B. J., Dawson, D. V., & Coughlin, J. A. (2008). Sunburns and risk of cutaneous melanoma: does age matter? A comprehensive meta-analysis. Annals of Epidemiology, 18(8), 614–627. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2008.04.006

lib.w: Plan your outdoor activities around the strongest midday sun and protect your skin
lib.d: every time you're out in strong sun
lib.t: Move walks, sport and outdoor time to the morning or late afternoon on sunny days, and cover up whenever you're outside for long.
lib.why: Planning around the strongest sun helps you enjoy being outdoors without getting burnt.

lib.w: Keep your headphones at around half volume
lib.t: Use your phone's volume limit or hearing-health setting, and take a listening break every hour or so.
lib.why: Keeping the volume moderate is a simple way to protect your hearing for the long term.
lib.ref: Dillard, L. K., Arunda, M. O., Lopez-Perez, L., Martinez, R. X., Jiménez, L., & Chadha, S. (2022). lib.w: Wear earplugs at concerts, clubs and other loud places
lib.t: Keep a pair of reusable earplugs in your bag or on your keys so you always have them with you.
lib.why: Earplugs at loud events protect your ears from temporary hearing loss and ringing afterwards.

lib.w: If you notice hearing difficulties, book a hearing test
lib.t: Signs include often asking people to repeat themselves or turning the TV up. A pharmacy, audiologist or your doctor can arrange a test, and if hearing aids are recommended, use them as advised.
lib.why: Getting your hearing checked keeps you connected and may help protect your thinking skills.

lib.w: Check the air quality index
lib.t: Most weather apps show it. On high-pollution days, exercise in a park, at a quieter time or indoors.
lib.why: Checking the air quality lets you keep enjoying outdoor exercise while limiting what you breathe in.
lib.ref: Chen, J., & Hoek, G. (2020). Long-term exposure to PM and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Environment International, 143, 105974. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105974

lib.w: Choose parks or quieter streets over busy roads
lib.d: on every walk, run or bike ride, where you can
lib.t: Plan your usual routes through parks, back streets or riverside paths, even if it adds a few minutes.
lib.why: Walking in green, quieter places may let you get more from your exercise than busy roads allow.

lib.t: Ventilate especially when cooking on a gas hob, and avoid burning candles or incense in closed rooms.
lib.why: Ventilating while cooking and limiting indoor burning cuts the smoke and fine particles you breathe.

lib.w: Learn a small new skill
lib.t: Try a few words in a new language, a new recipe, a song, a chord or a card trick.
lib.why: Learning something new keeps your mind active and is an easy, enjoyable habit to start.

lib.w: Practise a new skill that stretches you
lib.t: Choose something new to you, such as an instrument, a language or a craft, and practise it at the same time each week.
lib.why: Regularly stretching your mind with a new skill may help keep your memory sharp.

lib.d: for 1 hour, 4 days a week, building up gradually

lib.why: Getting properly good at a demanding new skill may help boost your memory.
